lesson.text: Quick memory: how often were the ancient Olympic Games held? (Every 4 years.) The Greeks also gave us ideas we still use every day. Today: democracy, theatre, maths and great thinkers.

Democracy comes from two Greek words: demos, the people, and kratos, power. So democracy means rule by the people. In Athens, about 508 BC, a leader called Cleisthenes changed the rules so that citizens, not one ruler, made the big decisions.

Citizens met on a hill called the Pnyx to decide the city's laws. Anyone could speak, then they voted by raising their hands. Juries of hundreds of citizens, picked by lot, decided trials, so nobody could buy their votes.

Only free men with Athenian parents were citizens, a small part of the people. Women, enslaved people and foreigners could not vote. Citizens could also vote to send a too-powerful man away for 10 years, by scratching his name on a bit of pottery.

Theatre grew from festivals for the god Dionysus. Actors, all men, wore masks. Tragedies told sad stories; comedies made people laugh, even at leaders. Theatres were cut into hillsides: Epidaurus seats about 14,000, and a whisper on stage reaches the back.

Greek thinkers loved maths. Pythagoras is remembered for a rule about right-angled triangles. Euclid wrote a geometry book that schools used for over 2,000 years. Archimedes worked out how levers lift heavy loads and why some things float.

Socrates taught by asking questions. His pupil Plato started a school called the Academy, and Plato's pupil Aristotle studied animals, plants and how to think clearly. The doctor Hippocrates taught that illnesses have natural causes.
Try it in the world: build an open-air theatre in a hillside, with rows of seats in a half circle. Then hold a vote with a show of hands. Next: the Persian Empire.

exercises.hint: Demos means the people; kratos means power.
exercises.explain: Demos + kratos: power to the people, rule by the people.

exercises.prompt: In Athens, citizens voted by raising their hands.
exercises.hint: Picture the meeting on the Pnyx.
exercises.explain: True: citizens raised their hands to vote on the city's laws.

exercises.prompt: What did Greek actors wear on their faces?
exercises.hint: The same actor could play a king, then a woman, then a god.
exercises.explain: Masks: one actor could play many parts, and the masks helped people far away see who was who.

exercises.prompt: Which city started democracy, about 508 BC?
exercises.explain: Athens, when Cleisthenes changed the rules about 508 BC.

exercises.hint: Think of how he made his pupils think.
exercises.explain: True: Socrates asked question after question to help people think clearly.

exercises.prompt: In Athens, women could vote on the city's laws.
exercises.explain: False: only free men with Athenian parents were citizens who could vote.

exercises.prompt: Match each Greek thinker to an idea.
exercises.hint: One was a doctor, one wrote about shapes, one asked questions, one studied floating.
exercises.explain: Archimedes: floating and levers. Euclid: geometry. Socrates: questions. Hippocrates: illnesses have natural causes.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: democracy in Athens then, or in most democracies now?
items: only men born to citizens vote
exercises.hint: Who could vote then, and who can vote now? How did they vote?
exercises.explain: Then: only some men, voting by raising hands on the Pnyx. Now: all adult citizens, women too, in a secret vote.

exercises.hint: It was a way nobody could fix in advance.
choices: by lot, like names drawn from a pot
exercises.explain: By lot: names were picked by chance, so nobody could choose or bribe the jury.

exercises.prompt: What was a piece of pottery with a name scratched on it used for?
exercises.hint: Athenians worried about anyone becoming too powerful.
choices: voting to send a powerful man away
exercises.explain: It was a vote to send a too-powerful man away from Athens for 10 years.

exercises.prompt: Why were Athenian juries so big and picked by lot?
exercises.hint: Could you bribe hundreds of people you did not know in advance?
choices: so nobody could buy their votes
exercises.explain: With hundreds of jurors picked by chance on the day, nobody could buy the verdict.

exercises.prompt: How was Athens' democracy different from most democracies today?
exercises.hint: Who was left out in Athens?
exercises.explain: In Athens only free men with Athenian parents could vote; today all adult citizens can.

exercises.prompt: Put these thinkers in order: each was the teacher of the next.
exercises.hint: Plato was Socrates' pupil, and Aristotle was Plato's.
exercises.explain: Socrates taught Plato, and Plato taught Aristotle.

exercises.prompt: An Athenian jury had 501 citizens. 263 voted 'guilty'. How many voted 'not guilty'?
exercises.hint: Every juror voted one way or the other: take the 'guilty' votes from the whole jury.

exercises.prompt: In a jury of 501, 263 votes is more than half.
exercises.explain: True: half of 501 is 250½, and 263 is more than that: a majority.

exercises.prompt: Sort the people of Athens: could they vote?
items: a free man with Athenian parents
exercises.hint: Only free men with Athenian parents were citizens.
exercises.explain: Could vote: free men with Athenian parents, like the citizen farmer. Could not: women, enslaved people and foreigners, which was most of the people in Athens.
